questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a padding oracle actually leaks
questions.learningObjective: State what information a padding oracle reveals
questions.stem: In a revision session, a student asks what a padding oracle actually reveals to an attacker. Which answer is right?

options.text: Whether the padding was valid, which leaks information about the plaintext bytes
The plaintext in full, one byte at a time
options.misconception: believes the oracle hands over plaintext directly

options.text: The encryption key, since padding is checked with it
options.misconception: confuses padding checks with key recovery

options.text: Nothing, since padding carries no information about the data

questions.explanation: An oracle that answers yes or no on padding validity still returns a signal, and repeated queries on modified ciphertexts turn that signal into knowledge of the plaintext bytes. The attacker never receives the plaintext itself, which is why the leak is easy to underestimate.
questions.hint: A yes or no answer is still a signal.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Which modes reveal the length of the plaintext
questions.learningObjective: Interpret repeated ciphertext blocks as revealed plaintext structure
questions.stem: In a revision sample, the first 16-byte block of a ciphertext appears three times in a row. What does the sample reveal about the plaintext?

options.text: The key was reused across three different messages
options.misconception: confuses block repetition with key reuse

options.text: The plaintext contains three identical blocks of 16 bytes
The encryption mode is a stream mode with a long keystream
The ciphertext was truncated after the first block

questions.explanation: A repeated ciphertext block means the same plaintext block was encrypted the same way again, so identical content is visible to anyone reading the ciphertext. The mode is a block mode rather than a stream mode, and no key reuse or truncation needs to be assumed.
questions.hint: Repeated ciphertext blocks mean repeated plaintext blocks.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a reused keystream gives away
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a reused keystream is worse than it first appears
questions.stem: Explain in revision notes why a reused keystream is a far bigger problem than the ciphertext suggests.

answer.exemplar: A reused keystream looks harmless at first because the ciphertext still looks random and the key never changes. But two messages encrypted with the same keystream can be XORed together, which cancels the keystream and leaves the XOR of the two plaintexts, so any structure in one message appears in the result. A single known plaintext then recovers the other message completely, and with a stream mode the keystream can be reused across many messages, so the damage scales with the archive.

questions.explanation: The visible randomness of the ciphertext hides a structural weakness, so the reuse has to be reasoned about rather than judged by appearance. Once the keystream cancels, one known plaintext exposes all the traffic under it.
questions.hint: XOR two ciphertexts and look at what is left.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a block cipher's block size means
questions.learningObjective: Compute how many blocks a record occupies once padded
questions.stem: A cipher with a 16-byte block encrypts a 100-byte record. How many blocks does it occupy, counting the final padded block?
questions.explanation: One hundred bytes is six full blocks of sixteen with four bytes left, so a seventh block carries the remainder and the padding. The padded size is 112 bytes, and the ciphertext length therefore reveals a range rather than the exact record length.
questions.hint: Divide by the block size and round up.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a key schedule has to prevent
questions.learningObjective: Identify the property shown by a key schedule description

stimulus.body: Revision notes on a block cipher show that the key schedule splits the 128-bit key into 4 words, rotates them through a fixed sequence, and adds a round constant to the first word of each round. Every round key differs from the previous one in every word.

questions.stem: Given the study notes, what property of the key schedule does this show?

options.text: Round keys are unrelated to one another, so recovering one gives little help
The cipher uses more rounds than the key schedule needs
The key is stored in a form that the hardware can use directly
options.misconception: assumes a storage property from the schedule

options.text: The schedule compensates for a weak block cipher underneath
options.misconception: invents a compensating role for the schedule

questions.explanation: A schedule that changes every word every round means no round key can be derived from another by simple relations, so an attacker who recovers one has little to work with. The notes show exactly this property and say nothing about round counts, storage or the underlying cipher.
questions.hint: Look at how much each round key changes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a bare key exchange leaves unestablished
questions.learningObjective: Choose the steps that close the gaps in a bare key exchange
questions.stem: Choose the first step and the last step for turning a bare key exchange into one that resists interception.

options.text: First: increase the group size; Last: rely on the key length
First: authenticate both parties' signatures; Last: bind the derived key to the transcript
First: encrypt the exchange with a password; Last: rotate the password monthly
options.misconception: prescribes a shared secret as an identity proof

options.text: First: add a nonce to each message; Last: send the nonce in the clear

questions.explanation: A bare exchange leaves the peer's identity and the transcript unestablished, so an attacker can relay it. Signing each party's contribution establishes identity, and binding the derived key to the full transcript closes the relay.
questions.hint: Identify the parties, then bind the transcript.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What certificate pinning makes hard
questions.learningObjective: State what certificate pinning makes hard for an attacker
questions.stem: A revision question asks what certificate pinning makes hard. Which answer is right?

options.text: It makes traffic interception impossible on the network
It makes certificate renewal easy when a supplier rotates
It makes it hard for a wrong or rogue authority to be accepted
It makes the client's own certificate harder to read

questions.explanation: Pinning restricts the client to a named key or certificate, so a misissued, coerced or compromised authority cannot slip in unnoticed. It does not defeat an attacker on the network path who holds the pinned private key, and it makes rotation a deliberate, planned task.

questions.topic: What a self-signed certificate establishes by itself
questions.learningObjective: Identify where trust comes from in a self-signed certificate deployment
questions.stem: A study group examines an internal site that uses a self-signed certificate. Which observation shows that trust here comes from outside the certificate chain?

options.text: The certificate was issued in 2019 and renewed twice
options.misconception: reads validity history as a trust source

options.text: The certificate lists the correct company name
options.misconception: treats a name claim as trust

options.text: The private key is stored in a hardware module
options.misconception: treats key custody as trust in the identity

options.text: The client compares the certificate against a copy embedded in the app

questions.explanation: A self-signed certificate proves only that its holder controls the matching private key. The trust in the identity comes from the comparison against an embedded copy, which is a separate out-of-band act that a substituted certificate cannot satisfy.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a padding oracle actually leaks
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a padding oracle is dangerous despite revealing no plaintext
questions.stem: Explain in revision notes why a padding oracle is dangerous even though it never returns any plaintext.

answer.exemplar: The oracle returns only a yes or no answer about padding validity, which looks harmless, but each answer narrows the possible values of the final plaintext byte, and by choosing modified ciphertexts an attacker can ask the question repeatedly until the byte is known. That converts a one-bit oracle into full plaintext recovery for most of the message, which is why a mode that reports padding errors must never be used to protect anything an attacker can submit to.

questions.explanation: Repeated adaptive queries turn a weak signal into full recovery, so the severity does not match the apparent amount of information returned. The defence is to remove the distinguishable error path or to check the tag before decrypting.
questions.hint: One bit, asked many times.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the ciphertext length produced by a stream-based mode
questions.stem: In a revision exercise, a stream-based mode encrypts a 37-byte message and the ciphertext is exactly the same length as the plaintext. How many bytes does the ciphertext occupy?
questions.explanation: A stream-based mode encrypts byte by byte, so a thirty-seven-byte message produces a thirty-seven-byte ciphertext with no padding. The ciphertext length therefore gives the exact message length to anyone who can see it.
questions.hint: The length is unchanged in this mode.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a reused keystream gives away
questions.learningObjective: Identify nonce reuse caused by a counter reset

stimulus.body: The group captured two ciphertexts from a stream-mode sender. Both were 96 bytes long and both were produced in the same minute. The notes also record that the sender's nonce counter was reset at midnight and the device had not restarted since.

questions.stem: Given the study notes, what is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The sender used a key that was too long for the messages
The two messages were encrypted with different keys
Both messages share the same nonce and therefore the same keystream
The device buffers messages and sends them in pairs

questions.explanation: A nonce counter reset at midnight reuses values for the same device and key, so the two messages share a nonce and therefore the keystream. XORing them would cancel the keystream and expose the relationship between the plaintexts.
questions.hint: Ask what a counter reset does to nonce values.

questions.topic: What a block cipher's block size means
questions.learningObjective: Choose the criteria for selecting between block sizes
questions.stem: A revision group must choose between an 8-byte block cipher and a 16-byte block cipher for a protocol. Choose the first criterion and the last criterion.

options.text: First: pick the larger block; Last: confirm the vendor is well known
options.misconception: chooses size first and a non-criterion last

options.text: First: pick the smaller block; Last: confirm it runs faster on the server
options.misconception: chooses on speed without regard to leakage

options.text: First: confirm both are approved; Last: pick whichever is faster
options.misconception: leaves the leakage question out entirely

options.text: First: consider how each leaks plaintext structure; Last: confirm the approved list allows it

questions.explanation: Block size decides how much plaintext structure can show up in the ciphertext, so that belongs in the decision before performance. A protocol also has to use a cipher on the approved list, but the leakage question is the one that belongs first.
questions.hint: Structure leakage first, approval second.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a key schedule has to prevent
questions.learningObjective: State what a key schedule has to prevent
questions.stem: A revision question asks what a key schedule has to prevent. Which answer is right?

options.text: That two different master keys produce the same or strongly related round keys
That the cipher runs for an unnecessarily large number of rounds
options.misconception: invents a limit on rounds as the goal

options.text: That the key is too long to store in hardware
options.misconception: confuses key length with schedule design

options.text: That the plaintext is longer than the block

questions.explanation: The schedule must spread every key bit across the round keys and keep distinct master keys far apart, so no two keys produce overlapping or related round keys. Rounds, storage size and message length are separate design choices that the schedule has no say over.
questions.hint: Ask what two different keys must not share.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a bare key exchange leaves unestablished
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a relayed exchange as an authentication failure
questions.stem: Revision notes record that a bare key exchange produced the same shared secret on both sides, yet a proxy sat in the middle and completed both halves without either side noticing. What does this show?

options.text: The exchange produced a weak shared secret value
options.misconception: confuses interception with a weak secret

options.text: Agreement on a secret does not establish who you are talking to
The group parameters used were too small for the task
The proxy could not decrypt the traffic
options.misconception: claims an outcome the notes do not support

questions.explanation: Both parties can hold the same secret and still be talking to an attacker who relayed the exchange, because nothing in a bare exchange ties the key to an identity or to the transcript. That unestablished binding is what lets the proxy sit in the middle unnoticed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What certificate pinning makes hard
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a pinned certificate changes about trust
questions.stem: Explain in a revision session what a pinned certificate changes about the trust decision.

answer.exemplar: Normally the client decides what to trust by following a chain to a root it already trusts, so any authority in that chain can be trusted to have checked the name. A pin replaces that chain with a single named certificate, so the client checks the server against the copy it holds and the root no longer has a say. That makes a misissued, coerced or compromised authority unable to slip in, at the cost of making every rotation an explicit, planned event.

questions.explanation: Pinning moves the trust decision from a chain of authorities to one named certificate held by the client, which is why it defeats a rogue authority. The trade is that rotation must be planned, since an unexpected new certificate is simply refused.
questions.hint: Trust moves from the chain to the copy you hold.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a self-signed certificate establishes by itself
questions.learningObjective: Compute the installed life of a pinned certificate
questions.stem: An app pins two certificates. Each is valid for 90 days, and the client is meant to replace a pin 30 days before it expires. For how many days can a pin remain installed under that rotation rule?
questions.explanation: Ninety days of validity minus the thirty day replacement window leaves sixty days that a pin is installed before the rotation window opens. That overlap is what allows both certificates to be trusted during a planned change.
questions.hint: Subtract the replacement window from the validity.

questions.topic: What a padding oracle actually leaks
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a padding oracle in a described service endpoint

stimulus.body: Revision notes on a service API: it accepts a base64 blob in a request body, decrypts it, and answers with either the decrypted content or the string 'invalid padding'. The notes mark this endpoint as reachable without authentication and record 2,000 requests to it in the last hour.

questions.stem: Given the study notes, what is the correct characterisation of this endpoint?

options.text: It is a padding oracle, and the reply distinguishes two outcomes for attacker-chosen input
It is harmless, because the replies are encrypted in transit
options.misconception: assumes transport hides a response difference

options.text: It leaks the key, since the padding check uses it
options.misconception: confuses a check with key recovery

options.text: It leaks only whether the request was authenticated

questions.explanation: The endpoint accepts attacker-chosen ciphertexts and returns a distinguishable verdict about padding, which is the definition of an oracle. Transport encryption does not hide a difference the application itself reveals, and no key or authentication is needed to exploit it.
questions.hint: Attacker-chosen input plus a visible verdict.

questions.topic: Which modes reveal the length of the plaintext
questions.learningObjective: Choose the steps that conceal message length
questions.stem: Choose the first step and the last step for keeping message length confidential on a link with fixed-size frames.

options.text: First: pad every message to the maximum; Last: publish the maximum
options.misconception: hides length only by using the largest size always

options.text: First: pad to a fixed frame size; Last: keep the frame size out of the protocol
First: compress the payload; Last: encrypt the compressed bytes
First: vary the padding per message; Last: send the padding length in clear
options.misconception: gives the attacker the length being hidden

questions.explanation: Fixed-size frames make every message occupy the same space, so an observer learns nothing about the content length. The frame size itself is not sensitive, and varying the padding while publishing its size would defeat the purpose entirely.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a reused keystream gives away
questions.learningObjective: State what a reused keystream gives an attacker
questions.stem: A revision question asks what a reused keystream gives away. Which answer is right?

options.text: The key itself, because the keystream is derived from it
options.misconception: confuses keystream reuse with key recovery

options.text: Nothing, as long as the ciphertext is encrypted correctly
options.misconception: assumes correct encryption implies no leakage

options.text: The XOR of the two plaintexts, and any known plaintext gives both
The length of the plaintext and nothing more
options.misconception: reduces the leak to length alone

questions.explanation: When two messages share a keystream, XORing the ciphertexts cancels the keystream and leaves the plaintexts XORed together. Recovering either plaintext then recovers the other, and a single known plaintext unlocks everything encrypted with that keystream.
questions.hint: Cancel the shared part out.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a block cipher's block size means
questions.learningObjective: Compare two block sizes for structure leakage
questions.stem: A revision table lists cipher A with a 16-byte block and cipher B with an 8-byte block. What follows from the comparison?

options.text: Cipher B encrypts faster because its blocks are smaller
Cipher B is more secure because it hides more structure
options.misconception: assumes smaller blocks mean more security

options.text: Cipher A cannot be used with modern modes
Cipher B's granularity of encryption is finer, so it leaks structure sooner

questions.explanation: A smaller block means less material is encrypted as one indivisible unit, so repeated plaintext structure shows up in the ciphertext more readily. Block size does not by itself decide speed or security, and neither cipher is excluded from modern modes by its block size.
questions.hint: Think about the unit of encryption.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a key schedule has to prevent
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a key schedule must achieve
questions.stem: Explain in revision notes what a key schedule must achieve and why.

answer.exemplar: The key schedule has to turn one master key into a distinct round key for every round, and it must do so in a way that spreads every key bit across all of them, so that an attacker who sees several round keys cannot work backwards to the master key or forwards to the others. It also has to keep distinct master keys from producing related round keys, since related round keys across two encryptions break the security the cipher was designed for.

questions.explanation: The schedule is where key material is spread and separated, and its failure modes are related round keys and easy backwards recovery from round keys. Rounds, key length and message length are chosen elsewhere and are not the schedule's business.
questions.hint: Spread the bits and keep keys apart.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a bare key exchange leaves unestablished
questions.learningObjective: Compare the public value sizes of two key exchange groups
questions.stem: A revision question compares group sizes: one exchange uses a 2048-bit group and another a 4096-bit group, and both produce a 256-bit shared secret. How many bits more are in the 4096-bit group's public value than in the 2048-bit group's?
questions.explanation: The public values differ by four thousand and ninety-six minus two thousand and forty-eight, which is two thousand and forty-eight bits. The shared secret stays 256 bits in both cases, so the group size governs the cost of an attack while the secret governs the strength of the result.
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller group size from the larger.

questions.topic: What certificate pinning makes hard
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an outage caused by an unplanned certificate rotation

stimulus.body: A mobile app hard-codes one server certificate and refuses to connect if the presented certificate does not match. Six months later the supplier rotated its certificate and the app stopped working for users for eleven days until a patch shipped with the new certificate.

questions.stem: Given the study notes, what does the outage demonstrate?

options.text: That the pinned certificate was defective
That certificate pinning should never be used in mobile apps
options.misconception: generalises one incident into a prohibition

options.text: That pinning makes rotation a client-side concern the supplier cannot change
That the transport layer failed to protect the session

The padding oracle leaks the whole key if queried often enough

questions.topic: Which modes reveal the length of the plaintext
questions.learningObjective: Compare plaintext length leakage between block and stream modes
questions.stem: Revision notes show that a block mode produced a 1,008-byte ciphertext for a 1,000-byte plaintext, while a stream mode produced exactly 1,000 bytes for the same input. What does this show?

options.text: The block mode compressed the plaintext by 24 bytes
The block mode rounds the length up to a block boundary, which the stream mode does not
The stream mode encrypted less of the message than the block mode
The block mode leaked the key length rather than the message length
options.misconception: confuses key length with plaintext length

questions.explanation: Block modes encrypt whole blocks, so the length of the plaintext is rounded up to the next boundary and the ciphertext is a little longer than the input. questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a reused keystream gives away
questions.learningObjective: Compare nonce reuse in a block mode and in a stream mode
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a reused nonce in a block mode and a reused nonce in a stream mode.

answer.exemplar: In a stream mode the nonce seeds a keystream, so reusing the nonce repeats the keystream exactly, and XORing two ciphertexts cancels it and exposes the relationship between the plaintexts. In a block mode a reused nonce makes the same block encrypt the same way twice, so the leak is that identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, which reveals structure but not the plaintext itself. The block mode weakness is weaker, but it is also easier to spot.

questions.explanation: The two cases fail in different ways: exact keystream reuse exposes plaintext relationships, while block repetition exposes structure. Only the stream case gives an attacker the XOR of two plaintexts directly.
questions.hint: Ask what is cancelled out, and what only repeats.

stimulus.body: Revision notes describe a cipher whose schedule adds a different round constant in each round, so that two different keys producing identical round keys in one round would differ in the next. The notes also record that the constants were chosen from a published table.

questions.stem: Given the study notes, what does the round constant contribute?

options.text: It separates encryptions that would otherwise share round key material
It makes the cipher's output longer than the block size
It lets the same key be used for two different messages safely
It proves the cipher is free from related key attacks

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What certificate pinning makes hard
questions.learningObjective: Compare pinning a leaf certificate with pinning an intermediate
questions.stem: A revision question asks how pinning interacts with an intermediate certificate. Which answer is right?

options.text: Pinning the intermediate certificate is as strong as pinning the leaf
options.misconception: ignores that the intermediate can be misused

options.text: Pinning removes the need for a valid chain to the root
Pinning the leaf removes the authority's role in the trust decision
Pinning has no effect once an intermediate is used

questions.explanation: Pinning a leaf certificate means the client checks that exact certificate, so the root and intermediates stop being part of the trust decision, which is the whole point when a misissuing authority is the concern. answer.exemplar: An attacker who can submit chosen ciphertexts and read the oracle's verdicts can recover the plaintext of the messages the oracle protects, byte by byte, and in many cases the last blocks are recovered exactly. Nothing, because the nonce was transmitted in the first packet

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What certificate pinning makes hard

questions.stem: Explain in revision notes why pinning and self-signing are different ideas.

answer.exemplar: A self-signed certificate describes who generated it and stops there, because its chain of trust ends with itself, so it establishes only control of the private key. Pinning is a client-side decision to trust one specific certificate whatever any authority says, and it can be applied to a properly issued certificate too. The two are independent: a pinned certificate may come from a trusted authority, and a self-signed certificate can be trusted only if the client pins it.

questions.explanation: Self-signing is a property of how the certificate was issued, while pinning is a property of how the client decides to trust. They can be combined or separated, and confusing them leads to false confidence in one or the other.
questions.hint: One is about issuance, the other is the client.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of related round keys
questions.stem: Explain in revision terms what happens when a key schedule produces related round keys.

answer.exemplar: If two different master keys produce related round keys, then an attacker who can observe encryptions under both keys may be able to cancel shared round-key material between the two encryptions, which is the same trick that breaks a reused keystream. The cipher then starts behaving like a cipher with a smaller effective key space than advertised, and the weakness grows the more rounds are involved, since there are more chances for a related-key relation to be exploited.

questions.explanation: Related round keys allow cancellation between encryptions, which is a structural failure rather than a matter of brute force. Keeping distinct master keys well separated is what prevents it.
questions.hint: Look for material shared between two encryptions.

questions.topic: What a reused keystream gives away
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a known plaintext yields full recovery
questions.stem: Explain in revision notes how a known plaintext turns a reused keystream into full recovery.

answer.exemplar: XORing the ciphertext with the known plaintext yields the keystream itself, byte for byte, because the keystream was the only unknown term in that equation. Once the keystream is known, every other message encrypted with it is read by XORing the same keystream against its ciphertext, and no further effort is needed per message. This is why reusing a keystream once is as damaging as reusing it many times, and why no amount of extra encryption on the later messages helps.

questions.explanation: One known plaintext exposes the keystream, and the keystream exposes everything else under it, so a single reuse ends the protection of the whole set. The chain is short enough that it is rarely appreciated before it happens.
questions.hint: Ciphertext XOR plaintext equals keystream.
